items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Motivation</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Dental enamel possesses a unique anisotropic, heterogeneous hierarchical structure which enables a combination of high hardness and remarkable durability compared to other natural and synthetic biomaterials. Nevertheless, it undergoes mechanical degradation through fracture from concentrated overloads and/or progressive wear, both of which can compromise tooth function and longevity. Enamel wear is of particular interest to anthropology, as it is ubiquitous and enables researchers to discern the culture, behaviors, and ecologies of the study populations. Studies simulating dental wear in vitro often employ simplified loading configurations based on combinations of axial and lateral forces, which successfully reproduce the “classical” microwear features of pits and scratches, but do not capture the full complexity of in vivo loading conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To conduct a preliminary in vitro investigation of previously underexplored rotationally induced occlusal mechanical wear in enamel.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cyclic contact tests combining compression (50 N) and rotation (30°) are applied to human enamel specimens using a testing machine with decoupled biaxial (axial‐torsion) actuators. Damage is characterized by electron and confocal microscopy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Rotational forces produce abrasive wear with distinct microscopic damage patterns, involving transitions from quasi‐plastic to brittle damage modes with an increasing number of contact cycles. After 10
                      <jats:sup>4</jats:sup>
                       cycles, the macrowear volume is 0.0023 mm
                      <jats:sup>3</jats:sup>
                      .
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Rotational microwear differs from “classical” pits and scratches associated with axial–lateral loading. Findings offer a framework for interpreting curved microscratches and provide a basis for future investigations. More broadly, they contribute to improving models of dental microwear and provide new insights in biomaterials science and anthropology.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
authors: Estíbaliz Sánchez‐González, Fernando Rodríguez‐Rojas, Paul J. Constantino, Michael A. Berthaume, Mark Hoffman, Óscar Borrero‐López

items.abstract: <jats:p>European colonization introduced abrupt changes into the Americas. These included the introduction of infectious diseases, forced labor and displacement of Indigenous and African individuals, European settlement, and the imposition of caste regimes. However, the role of these forces in reshaping communities across different regions remains debated. This is especially true in the Virreinato del Río de la Plata (the territories of present-day Argentina, Bolivia, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Brazil), which is less studied than other regions such as the United States, the Caribbean, and Mexico. We investigated how these forces shaped the colonial societies of Mendoza in the Cuyo region (Central-Western Argentina) by sequencing ancient DNA of 28 individuals (17th to 19th centuries) excavated from churches associated with different social strata, recovering 22 mitochondrial genomes, and genome-wide data of 15 individuals. By performing paleogenomic analyses contextualized by burial site, we detected admixture among Indigenous, European, and African populations, with ancestry partially structured by church and burial location. Exceptions to this pattern indicate social mobility and flexible social classifications beyond genetic ancestry. The European-related ancestry aligns with Southern European migration, while African-related ancestry shows affinities to Western-Central Africa. The Indigenous-related ancestry shows highest affinity to precontact populations from Cuyo, supporting local genetic continuity across the colonial period. Additionally, uniparental markers reflect sex-biased dispersal and admixture. These findings reveal often-neglected African contributions to the city’s formation and illustrate how caste, labor, and migration shaped colonial urban societies. Our work provides a scalable model for interrogating caste regimes, social mobility, and admixture in understudied regions of the Americas.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>How the life of prehistoric people was influenced by climate change and extreme events often remains elusive. Finding appropriate spatiotemporal scales is the major challenge for studies with socioenvironmental questions. This challenge can be overcome by sourcing climatic information from archaeological sites, alongside traces of human agency. For instance, extreme cold-events have been proposed as causing a standstill in early farming expansion across the Mediterranean 8600-8000 years ago. However, there is no immediate (local/short-term) evidence of such events and how they might have influenced people’s lives, nor have previous records been sufficiently resolved to test this robustly. Here we statistically assess the influence of on-site and short-term extremes on human decision-making hypothesized by long-term climate records. Using the largest dataset yet of high-resolution temperature archives in mollusks, we test whether early farmers would have been exposed to extreme cold-events, compromising their subsistence by reducing harvest yields. This immediate agricultural risk is argued to have prevented the spread of new settlements and thus delayed the vigorous expansion that followed, one of prehistory’s fastest known dispersals. Direct comparison of paleotemperature and subsistence data from the same archaeological contexts shows no winter cooling of the magnitude proposed for this period, and no strong relationship between climate and subsistence. Our study reveals how a major scale mismatch in climate-society research can be resolved at the site level, integrating climatic variability on the subannual timescale crucial to farming, and provides a direct, local empirical test of a long-assumed climate impact.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Detailed information on the cardiac morphology of the scarlet ibis (
                    <jats:italic>Eudocimus ruber</jats:italic>
                    ) remains limited. This study aimed to characterize the gross and microscopic anatomy of this species' heart and provide morphometric data. We examined six specimens (three males and three females) using gross anatomical analysis, morphometry, conventional radiography, three‐dimensional scanning, light microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. The mean heart mass was 5.93 ± 1.49 g (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 6), corresponding to 1.10 ± 0.23% of body mass, and the mean radiographic cardiothoracic ratio was 66.90 ± 5.78% (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 3). Macroscopic examination identified three venae cavae: the right and left cranial venae cavae and the caudal vena cava. The left atrioventricular valve had two cusps with chordae tendineae and papillary muscles, whereas the right atrioventricular valve had a single muscular fold. Histological examination identified uninucleated and binucleated Purkinje fibers in the subendocardial region, extending into myocardial muscle bundles. The base of the aorta showed hyaline cartilage containing chondrocytes and chondroblasts, with no bone tissue identified in the examined sections. These findings provide anatomical, morphometric, and histological data on the heart of
                    <jats:italic>E. ruber</jats:italic>
                    and a basis for future comparative studies of avian cardiac morphology.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Beatriz Rosa Silva, Maria Gabriela Aparecida Farias Pereira, Max Alex Santos Ferreira, Júlia Vaz Feio, Elane Guerreiro Giese, Érika Branco, Antônio Basílio Guerreiro Junior, Ana Rita de Lima
